blocking.section: Benchmark methodology (Scenarios, O1 arithmetic); Throughput and resources per core (Throughput targets); Budget philosophy (PB-11)
blocking.issue: O1 now reaches the ceiling, but the PB-11 derivation is still wrong, and it rests on an S3 figure that cannot hold. (1) The arithmetic charges 20,000 rejections/s. Rejections are offered minus goodput, so at the claimed 92% (36,800 rps) there would be 23,200/s. The fixed point is G = (4 vCPU - 60,000 x 16 us) / (100 us - 16 us), about 36,190 rps, which is 90.5% of saturation, not 92%. That leaves 0.5 points of margin. (2) The 16 us is the rejection's p50, but CPU is consumed at the mean. The p99 is 40 us, so the mean is likely above p50. At an 18 us mean, G is about 35,610 rps (89%), which fails PB-11. (3) S3 runs the S2 chain (auth.jwt and ratelimit) and adds TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2. Yet it claims 40,000 rps saturation, which is 100 us per request, against S2's 32,000 rps (125 us per request) on cleartext HTTP/1.1. Go's HTTP/2 server adds a goroutine handoff per stream and serializes writes through the serve loop, so TLS plus HTTP/2 being 20% cheaper per request than cleartext HTTP/1.1 is implausible without a derivation. O1a's '2.2 vCPU', O1b's 60,000 rps offered load and the 0.54 s queueing figure all inherit the 100 us.

blocking.fix: Derive S3 from S2's per-request CPU plus TLS record and HTTP/2 framing adders (hypothesis). For example, about 18 us more gives about 143 us per request and 28,000 rps or more (target). If you keep S3 above S2, show the syscall-amortization numbers that justify it. Give the RZ-RT-005 rejection a mean CPU budget, for example 16 us or less mean (target), measured by the component benchmark, instead of using only p50. Then recompute O1 with G = (C - O x r) / (s - r). With S3 at 143 us, O1b offers 42,000 rps and goodput is about 26,200 rps, which is 93.7% (target) and closes PB-11 with margin. Recompute O1a's CPU (about 3.0 vCPU) and the queueing time (20,000 / G, about 0.76 s, hypothesis), and update OQ-performance-budgets-and-benchmarking-11 to match. If no figure closes, lower PB-11 and show the arithmetic.

blocking.section: Benchmark suite and CI gating (Suite layers, Latency job budget)
blocking.issue: Regression introduced by the L1-6 fix: the 75-minute rotation slots cannot hold what is assigned to them under the document's own duration and gating rules. The Macro p99 gate runs every scenario 'on its night' as an interleaved A/B. The Duration rule then makes each A/B scenario cost 10 runs of 180 s plus 10 warm-ups of 60 s, which is 40 minutes (the S1 and S2 line confirms this: 80 minutes for two). So the 'S3 and S5' slot needs 80 minutes or more, and the 'S6, S6n and S7' slot needs 120 minutes or more, against 75. The saturation-ladder slot needs about 21 steps of 60 s per scenario, starting from 5%, for up to six scenarios (S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S7), plus the PB-15 and PB-16 points: over 2 hours. The 170-minute total also assumes the minimum 60 s warm-up. Warm-up may extend to 180 s, which alone takes S1 and S2 to 120 minutes, and an invalid run re-runs once. So the Latency job can exceed Testing's 3-hour limit, and the claim that each item runs 'at least weekly' fails.

blocking.fix: Publish a slot table sized from the duration rule. Each A/B scenario costs 40 minutes nominal and 60 minutes with the maximum warm-up. Put at most one A/B scenario per 75-minute slot, filled with absolute-criteria runs (O1, O2, C1, C2, R1, G1). Start the ladders at 50% of expected saturation (about 13 steps) and split them across slots. The result is about 11 or 12 slots, so state 'each item runs at least every two weeks (target)', or give the rotating scenarios a shorter A/B design with the statistics consequence stated. Cap warm-up so the worst case, including one re-run of one scenario, fits 180 minutes, and show that worst-case sum. Record the change under OQ-performance-budgets-and-benchmarking-3.
